dekker_mutex.doc: Dekker's algorithm: flags plus a turn, with the polite yield when both sides are interested.
dekker_mutex.name: dekker_mutex
dekker_mutex.note: The first correct software solution to mutual exclusion, and it is written for exactly two processes.

monitor_fifo_mutex.doc: The same Mesa monitor, except that a notified thread is handed into the monitor's entry queue instead of racing for the lock.
monitor_fifo_mutex.name: monitor_fifo_mutex
monitor_fifo_mutex.note: Prove the mutex correct with a fair entry queue and it stays correct; the verdict below is about the queue, not the condition variable.

monitor_mesa_mutex.doc: A Mesa monitor used as a mutex: busy is re-tested in a loop, not an if.
monitor_mesa_mutex.name: monitor_mesa_mutex
monitor_mesa_mutex.note: The re-acquire at the top of the loop is what makes a lost signal harmless.

peterson_mutex.doc: Peterson's algorithm: the same two flags, with the turn doing the yielding instead of a busy loop.
peterson_mutex.name: peterson_mutex
peterson_mutex.note: Shorter and easier to prove than Dekker, and still strictly a two-process solution.

rw_barrier.doc: Two symmetric gates: the first reader closes wgate, the first writer closes rgate, and each phase drains before the other opens.
rw_barrier.name: rw_barrier
rw_barrier.note: The barrier stops new readers once a writer has declared. It does not by itself force the phases to alternate; the verdicts below say how far it actually gets.

rw_broken_count.doc: Readers preference with the guard off by one: the first reader tests rd == 0 instead of rd == 1.
rw_broken_count.name: rw_broken_count
rw_broken_count.note: One comparison away from a correct solution, and safety is gone. This is why the count has to be read while the mutex is held.
rw_broken_count.truncated: stopped at the first safety violation

rw_dekker.doc: The readers-preference pattern with Dekker's algorithm guarding the reader count instead of the section.
rw_dekker.name: rw_dekker
rw_dekker.note: The pattern really is independent of the lock underneath it -- Dekker works as well as a semaphore here, at the price of a busy wait.

rw_dekker_2readers.doc: Two readers and no writer, with Dekker's algorithm guarding the count.
rw_dekker_2readers.name: rw_dekker_2readers
rw_dekker_2readers.note: Both readers end up inside at once, which is the whole point of the problem -- and which no plain mutex, Dekker's included, can do.

rw_fair.doc: A FIFO turnstile: a writer waiting for wrt holds queue, so no new reader can slip in ahead of it.
rw_fair.name: rw_fair
rw_fair.note: The writer pays for fairness by holding a semaphore across its whole wait.

rw_monitor_fifo.doc: The same monitor, except that a woken thread queues for the monitor lock instead of racing newcomers for it.
rw_monitor_fifo.name: rw_monitor_fifo
rw_monitor_fifo.note: One change, and the fairness verdict flips: what was missing was never the condition variable, it was the entry queue.

rw_monitor_mesa.doc: Readers and writers as one condition variable inside one monitor: the monitor lock is taken for the bookkeeping, the condition variable for the waiting.
rw_monitor_mesa.name: rw_monitor_mesa
rw_monitor_mesa.note: Every wait loops back to the re-test, which is what Mesa semantics demand; a lost signal is then simply harmless, and notifyAll is what lets a whole read phase through at once.

rw_readers_pref.doc: The classic first solution: a mutex protects the reader count, wrt excludes writers.
rw_readers_pref.name: rw_readers_pref
rw_readers_pref.note: Readers never wait for a waiting writer, so a writer can be overtaken for ever.
